summary:
Guyana is one of five countries in the Western Hemisphere that still criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Sections 352 to 354 of the Criminal Law Act create offences of gross indecency and attempted buggery, and buggery carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment. Prosecutions are rare, but the provisions anchor stigma against LGBT people and give police a vocabulary of threat.

No legal gender recognition exists. The direct anti-cross-dressing offence, section 153(1)(xlvii) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act, derived from an 1893 statute, was struck down by the Caribbean Court of Justice in November 2018 in McEwan v Attorney General, which held it unconstitutionally vague and a violation of freedom of expression. The challenge was filed in 2010 with SASOD after trans women were arrested in 2009 and held for three nights under the same provision.

Violence against trans women is documented and persistent. At the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights' 191st session in Washington in November 2024, a hearing requested by the Guyana Equality Forum heard testimony from Blossom Inc., SASOD and the Guyana Sex Work Coalition on the impact of gender-based violence on migrant women, sex workers and trans women; Commission chair Roberta Clarke called on Guyana to take urgent action. The record carries 69 documented cases of violence against trans women between 2018 and 2022.

The justice system has failed trans complainants directly. In January 2017 trans woman Petronella Trotman was stabbed in Georgetown with scissors, sustaining a neck wound, and pelted with glass bottles. When the matter came before magistrate Dylon Bess on 2 March 2017, she was told to "dress like a man," refused entry to the courtroom, and the case was dismissed; the prosecution had rested on the 1893 cross-dressing offence, whose "improper purpose" test left the outcome to the magistrate's discretion.

Policing remains a risk in its own right. SASOD documented in May 2019 that officers use residual clauses of the Summary Jurisdiction Act to extort LGBT people, threatening men found in "compromising positions" with arrest to extract bribes, harassing same-sex couples at seawalls and parks, and leaving complainants who file formal reports to face secondary discrimination at stations and give watered-down accounts. Loitering and vagrancy provisions remain usable against LGBT populations, particularly sex workers.

Public attitudes have shifted measurably: a 2022 poll recorded 72% acceptance, with hostility 13 percentage points lower than in 2013. Five of six parties in the 2025 general election, including the ruling party, backed decriminalisation, though no repeal has followed. There is no anti-discrimination legislation; the UN Human Rights Committee called for such legislation in April 2024. A small organised community operates in Georgetown through SASOD and allied groups.
tangentialFactors:
Decriminalisation has cross-party political cover rather than opponents: five of the six parties contesting the 2025 election, the ruling party among them, campaigned in favour of repealing the same-sex conduct provisions, which places the barrier to reform in legislative scheduling rather than declared policy.

Public opinion is no longer the obstacle it was a decade ago. The 2022 acceptance figure of 72% and the 13-point fall in hostility since 2013 suggest a social climate more permissive than the statute book implies, which bears on how much risk a visibly trans visitor attracts in public space.

The 2018 Caribbean Court of Justice judgment is the template for challenging vague morality offences in the region, and it removed the single provision most likely to be used against a trans person in the street or a public building. What it did not touch are the residual Summary Jurisdiction clauses that police continued to invoke after the ruling.

Sustained legal advocacy exists and is well connected internationally: SASOD brought the McEwan challenge, its officers testify before the Inter-American Commission, and Guyana Equality Forum secured the November 2024 hearing. Allied groups including Blossom Inc. and the Guyana Sex Work Coalition work on violence against trans women specifically.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition; official documents continue to reflect sex assigned at birth, with no statute or procedure permitting amendment.

The 2009 arrests of trans women under the 1893 cross-dressing offence, which produced three nights in detention, were the trigger for the litigation filed in 2010 with SASOD that succeeded in 2018. Trans Guyanese were therefore exposed to that offence for the eight years the challenge was pending.

Police extortion of LGBT residents documented in 2019 targeted people in "compromising positions" and same-sex couples in public places such as seawalls and parks. Residents who lodge formal complaints encounter secondary discrimination at police stations, which suppresses reporting and leaves assaults uninvestigated.

Sex workers bear a disproportionate share of residual enforcement, since loitering and vagrancy clauses remain in force after the 2018 judgment and are applied to them as LGBT people.

Community infrastructure is concentrated in Georgetown: SASOD, alongside Blossom Inc. and the Guyana Sex Work Coalition, provides the advocacy, documentation and litigation capacity available to residents.

Attitudes among residents improved between 2013 and 2022, with 72% acceptance recorded in the later poll, and five of six political parties in the 2025 election, the ruling party included, publicly backed decriminalisation.
outOfScopeNotes:
How often sections 352 to 354 of the Criminal Law Act are actually charged is unresolved here: sources describe buggery prosecutions as rare but give no case counts or dates for the current period.

The provenance of the figure of 69 documented cases of violence against trans women between 2018 and 2022 is not established in the sources at hand; it appears as the figure cited in connection with the November 2024 Inter-American Commission hearing, and the underlying dataset is not identified.

Whether police opened or concluded any investigation into the January 2017 attack on Petronella Trotman after the courtroom exclusion is not sourced; the record shows the summary charge was dismissed and does not follow the matter further.

No source in the inventory records whether a decriminalisation bill has been introduced or scheduled for a vote since the 2025 election positions, nor whether any gender-recognition legislation has been drafted. Both remain unresolved rather than confirmed absent.

Enforcement of residual Summary Jurisdiction clauses after 2019 is described through SASOD's documentation of that year; the current frequency of such extortion or harassment is not sourced.
